proof_skeleton_nl: For the lower bound, use the explicit quadratic function g(n)=n^2. A direct calculation shows g(g(n))=n^4 and g(n+1)-g(n)=2n+1, and the elementary inequality 2n+1 >= n^{4r} for every r <= 1/4 gives admissibility; in particular r=1/4 works. For the upper bound, fix r>1/4 and assume a witness g exists. Because r>=0, the right-hand side is always at least 1, so g must be strictly increasing and satisfy g(n)>=n. Summing the original inequality from k=n to k=g(n)-1 yields the valid interval estimate g(g(n))-g(n) >= (g(n)-n)(g(g(n)))^r, hence g(g(n))^{1-r} >= g(n)-n. The dedicated impossibility lemma L5 rules out the coexistence of strict increase, the original inequality, and this interval estimate when r>1/4. Therefore no exponent larger than 1/4 is admissible. Combining this with the explicit witness at r=1/4 shows that 1/4 is the largest possible constant.

steps.derives: The real number \(\tfrac14\) is admissible: there exists a function \(g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\), namely \(g(n)=n^2\), such that for every \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), \(g(n+1)-g(n) \ge (g(g(n)))^{1/4}\).
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L2 with r = 1/4. This gives an explicit witness function and therefore shows 1/4 belongs to the admissible set.

steps.derives: Fix an arbitrary real number \(r > \tfrac14\). Assume for contradiction that there exists \(g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\) such that \(g(n+1)-g(n) \ge (g(g(n)))^r\) for every \(n\). Then \(g\) is strictly increasing, and in particular \(g(n) \ge n\) for every \(n\).
steps.trivial_justification: Since r > 1/4 implies r >= 0, L3 applies directly to the hypothetical witness g.

steps.derives:
For the same hypothetical function \(g\) from A2, one has for every \(n \in \mathbb{N}\)
\[
g(g(n)) - g(n) \ge (g(n)-n)(g(g(n)))^r,
\]
and hence also
\[
g(g(n))^{1-r} \ge g(n)-n.
\]
steps.trivial_justification: A2 supplies the strict increase required by L4, and the original inequality is part of the contradiction hypothesis. Therefore all hypotheses of L4 are satisfied.

steps.derives: The contradiction hypothesis from A2 is impossible when \(r > \tfrac14\). Therefore, for every real \(r > \tfrac14\), there is no function \(g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\) satisfying \(g(n+1)-g(n) \ge (g(g(n)))^r\) for all \(n\).
steps.trivial_justification: A2 gives that any hypothetical witness for r > 1/4 is strictly increasing. A3 gives that the same witness also satisfies the extra interval inequality \(g(g(n))^{1-r} \ge g(n)-n\) for all n. L5 states that no strictly increasing function can satisfy both of these global conditions when r > 1/4. Hence the assumed witness cannot exist. Because the initial choice of r > 1/4 was arbitrary, every exponent strictly larger than 1/4 is inadmissible.

steps.derives:
The largest real constant \(r\) such that there exists a function \(g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\) with
\[
g(n+1)-g(n) \ge (g(g(n)))^r
\]
for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) is exactly \(\tfrac14\).
steps.trivial_justification: Define the admissible set S exactly as in L6. Step A1 proves 1/4 ∈ S. Step A4 proves every r > 1/4 is not in S. Applying L6 yields that 1/4 is the largest admissible real number, which is exactly the root theorem statement.
